sections.h2: How Kansas property tax is calculated
sections.html:
A Kansas tax bill comes in two steps. The county appraiser's estimate of fair market value, multiplied by an assessment rate, gives the assessed value. Take that assessed figure, apply the mill levy, and divide by 1,000 to arrive at the tax.

The residential assessment rate is 11.5%. Commercial property is assessed at 25% of full value. One mill means $1 in tax on every $1,000 of assessed value. The levy stacks up the rates of every local taxing body, such as the school district, county and city. The county clerk can tell you the levy for your address.

The state's own teaching example uses a $200,000 home and a combined levy of 130 mills. Treat that as an illustration of the method, not a forecast for any particular house.

A Kansas tax year opens with valuation notices by March 1 and closes with the second-half payment on May 10 of the next year. Sellers and owners should watch the dates below.

Kansas property tax calendar for real estate
DateEvent
March 1County sends valuation notices
30 days from mailingFinal day to start an equalization appeal with the county appraiser
May 15Deadline for the informal meeting with the appraiser
May 20Appraiser issues the final determination
June 1Appraiser sends certified values to the clerk
August 25Budgets go to the clerk from each governing body
November 1Clerk hands the tax roll to the treasurer
December 20Payment in full, or the first half, is due
May 10Second half comes due

Personal property runs on a separate schedule, and its valuation notices are dated May 1. If you sell a house that includes a mobile home, a boat or business equipment, ask the county which schedule each item falls under.

sections.h2: What to check on your valuation notice
sections.html:
The notice that arrives by March 1 is your only cheap chance to challenge the number. Read the appraised value first and ask whether it matches what similar homes near you would sell for. Then look at the dates, because the clock for an equalization appeal starts on the mailing date printed on the notice, not the day it reaches your mailbox.

If the value looks high, call the county appraiser before the informal meeting date and ask what data supports it. Bring photos of any damage, repair estimates, and a recent appraisal if you have one. A seller with an old roof or a cracked foundation has a better case when the paperwork is in the file.

Every taxing unit writes its own levy from its budget. The revenue neutral rate is the mill levy that, applied to the current year's assessed valuation, would produce the same property tax revenue as the prior year.

Public steps are built into the calendar around it. The county clerk reports the rate for each taxing jurisdiction by June 15. A governing body that wants to go above it tells the county clerk by July 20 and holds a public hearing between August 20 and September 20. That hearing window is the best time for a homeowner to speak up about a rising bill, because budgets are certified by August 25.

The levy is one reason two houses with the same appraised value can carry different bills. A house in one school district or city can sit under a higher combined levy than a house a few blocks away in another. Buyers compare tax bills across neighborhoods, so learn your own levy before you settle on an asking price. Your county clerk can give you the number, and your last tax statement shows what you paid.

You have two routes, and for a given tax year you must choose one: an equalization appeal after the spring notice, or payment under protest when you pay.

  • Equalization appeal: call the county appraiser within a month of the date the notice was mailed, then go to the informal meeting, which must happen by May 15.
  • Third-party appraisal option: after the informal result, the owner may file a fee simple appraisal done by a Kansas certified appraiser inside 60 days after the notice went out. The county then has 90 days to respond.
  • Payment under protest: hand the protest form to the county treasurer at the time you pay. December 20 is the cutoff, even if you are paying only the first half.

An informal meeting that fails to settle things sends you on to the Board of Tax Appeals. Single-family homes go to the BOTA Small Claims Division first. So does any non-agricultural property valued under $3 million. One hearing officer hears small claims appeals, and the appeal form usually comes with the notice of informal meeting results. Each filing deadline is 30 days after the earlier decision was mailed.

sections.h2: What happens when the tax goes unpaid
sections.html:
Unpaid Kansas real estate tax draws interest and, after enough time, can lead to a county foreclosure sale. K.S.A. 79-2004 gives two choices: pay it all by December 20, or pay half then and half on May 10. Weekend deadlines roll forward to Monday or the next business day. Tiny bills of $10 or less cannot be split and are due whole on December 20.

Miss the first half and interest starts at the K.S.A. 79-2968 rate, with five percentage points added each year. Any balance left after May 10 keeps drawing that same rate, and the meter runs until you pay or the county forecloses and sells the property.

Foreclosure comes later. Under K.S.A. 79-2801, when property the county bought at sale remains unredeemed on September 1 of the second year afterward, the county attorney is directed to file an action in district court. The law makes that action discretionary where the aggregate assessed valuation is under $300,000 or the delinquent taxes and special assessments are under $10,000. If the county does not act on property inside a city and the taxes have stayed delinquent for three years after the property became eligible, the city may start the foreclosure itself.

If a delinquency notice has already arrived, read it closely and call the county treasurer right away about redemption. Waiting costs money, because interest keeps building every year the balance sits open, and a sale that is still weeks away can be derailed by a lien nobody planned for.

sections.h2: If you owe tax when you sell
sections.html:
The closing agent normally pays the current year's tax plus any arrears from your sale proceeds. Because a tax lien stays with the property, it must be cleared before a buyer can take clean title. Get a payoff number from the title company well ahead of closing day.

  • The recorded deed must show the buyer's name and mailing address. The register of deeds passes that address to the county clerk so tax statements reach the right person (K.S.A. 58-2221).
  • A deed generally needs a sales validation questionnaire. K.S.A. 79-1437f keeps sale prices off the public record.
  • Questions about a specific property's value belong with the county appraiser, and the county treasurer answers payment questions.

If a house has delinquent taxes, a repair backlog or a probate hold, our team can look at it as-is. A title company will ask about the same tax points, so have your latest tax statement in hand when you call.

Before you list, collect the newest valuation notice and tax statement, confirm what has been paid, and find out whether an appeal or protest is still open.

faqs.q: When are Kansas property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax is due in full by December 20, or in two halves with the first by December 20 and the second by May 10 of the next year (K.S.A. 79-2004). A due date on a weekend moves to the next business day.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Kansas valuation?
faqs.a: Thirty days from the date the county mailed the notice of value. The notice goes out by March 1, so the window usually closes in spring. The informal meeting with the county appraiser must be held by May 15.

faqs.q: Can I appeal and also pay under protest?
faqs.a: No. A taxpayer picks one path for the same tax year: appeal at the valuation notice or pay under protest, not both.

faqs.q: What is the residential assessment rate in Kansas?
faqs.a: Residential property is assessed at 11.5% of appraised value. The assessed value is then multiplied by the combined mill levy and divided by 1,000 to produce the tax.

faqs.q: Who do I contact about my Kansas property tax bill?
faqs.a: The county appraiser handles value questions, the county clerk holds the mill levy, and the county treasurer takes payments and the payment under protest form.
